Who keeps property records in Miami-Dade County

The Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller serves as county recorder. Under Chapter 28 of the Florida Statutes, the clerk records every instrument the law allows to be recorded here.

The Official Records hold deeds, mortgages, liens, certain affidavits, subdivision plats, judgments, declarations of domicile, satisfactions and releases, powers of attorney and financial statements. Fees and transfer taxes are figured and collected when a document is recorded.

Searching Miami-Dade Official Records

The clerk's online Official Records search covers every instrument above. Search by name, or by book and page when you already have a reference.

  • Name searches work for grantors, grantees and lienholders. Try every spelling of a name, and add the folio number when you have it.
  • Credit bureaus pick up liens and judgments recorded here. If a bureau reports one you do not recognize, ask for its book and page and request a copy from the Records Library.
  • The clerk runs a free fraud alert that notifies an owner within a day whenever a deed or mortgage is filed against the owner's name.

Recording fees

Most documents cost $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page. A lis pendens costs $5 for the first page and $4 for each additional page.

Why the county fee differs from the state statute

Florida's clerk fee statute prints $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page of an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches, plus $1.00 for each name beyond four. It adds a $1.00 modernization charge on the first page and $0.50 on later pages, and an extra $4 per page for technology.

Plats run $30.00 for the first page and $15.00 for each added page, and processing a tax deed application costs $60.00. The Miami-Dade clerk publishes all-in figures, which is why the county's first-page fee reads $10. Give your title agent the clerk's current schedule instead of adding the statute lines yourself.

Documentary stamp tax on a deed

Deed stamps are 60 cents per $100 of consideration, rounded up to the next hundred. Miami-Dade is the only county that uses 60 cents in place of the standard 70.

A separate surtax of 45 cents per $100 applies to transfers of real property other than a single-family residence. Mortgages pay 35 cents per $100 of the note, plus intangible tax of $2 per $1,000.

Every party to a deed is liable for the tax under state rules, whoever agrees to pay. Your contract with the buyer sets the practical split.

What goes on a mortgage, satisfaction or lien filing

Mortgage filings must be original, signed and notarized. Attach a copy of the note, or write the note amount across the face of the mortgage. The filing needs addresses for lender and borrower and a Prepared By line.

  • A satisfaction or release needs the book and page of the mortgage, the holder's signature and a notarized acknowledgement.
  • An assignment of mortgage needs the book and page, the assignor's signature and a notary.
  • A construction lien needs the lienor's signature, a notary and a legal description or property address.

A seller paying off a loan should confirm the satisfaction is recorded, then search Official Records to see it indexed.

Special deeds and court sales

A quit claim deed, a deed given in place of foreclosure and a contract for deed are all on the revenue department's list of taxable documents. An executor's deed under a probated will is treated as not taxable.

A foreclosure certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid. A lis pendens, the notice that a foreclosure suit is pending, records at $5 for the first page. Searching for one early can warn a buyer that a lender has gone to court. In any distressed transfer, pull the title record before signing so every lien is in view.

What a Miami-Dade deed must include

The clerk's deed checklist is specific, and a missing item gets a document returned.

  • An original document with the seller's signature.
  • Addresses for grantors and grantees.
  • Two witnesses not related to the transaction, with each name and post office address printed beneath the signature.
  • A full notary acknowledgement.
  • A Prepared By statement with name and address.
  • Documentary stamps, plus the property transfer form.
  • A folio number, which is encouraged but not required, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Section 689.01 of the Florida Statutes separately requires two subscribing witnesses on a conveyance.

Filing in person, by mail or electronically

There are four routes. Bring the original and fees to the Osvaldo N. Soto Miami-Dade Justice Center, mail it to the Office of County Recorder at 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, FL 33128, use an approved eRecording vendor, or use the clerk's eRecording Web Service for Notices of Commencement and Declarations of Domicile.

Electronic filings take roughly 1 to 3 business days, excluding weekends and holidays, before they appear online. Same-day recording is not promised, so bring time-sensitive documents in person.

Cash is accepted only in person. Credit cards are in person only, with a $5,000 daily limit.

Removing a Social Security number from a public record

You can ask. The clerk accepts requests to redact Social Security, bank account and credit card numbers from documents that are available online, using its online redaction form with the file number or book and page.

People covered by Chapter 119 exemptions can file a confidentiality request, in person or online. Party names stay in the index unless the name includes a street address, as in some trusts or LLCs.

Before you record or sell

Miami-Dade has 1,125,274 housing units, and the filing load is heavy, so a clean document matters. Compare the folio and legal description with your prior deed, line up witnesses and a notary before the signing, and confirm the fees with the clerk on the day. After closing, search Official Records under your name to see that the deed and any satisfaction appear.

If you need a copy of a recorded item for a lender or title agent, ask the clerk for a certified copy rather than printing a search screen. Keep the recorded copy of your deed, the settlement statement and any payoff letters together in one folder for later tax and title questions.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I file a deed in Miami-Dade?

At the County Recorder's Office, 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, or through an approved eRecording vendor. The clerk accepts mail and in-person filings as well.

What does the clerk charge to file a Miami-Dade deed?

The clerk lists $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, before documentary stamps. The state statute prints a lower base and allows other charges on top, so quote the clerk's list.

Does Miami-Dade charge a deed surtax on a house?

The 45 cents per $100 surtax applies to real property other than a single-family residence, so a deed for only a single-family home does not carry it.

Do I have to record a deed after a sale?

Recording gives the public notice of the transfer. Ask the title agent to record promptly, and search Official Records afterward to confirm the deed appears.

How long does eRecording take in Miami-Dade?

Roughly 1 to 3 business days before the document is viewable online.

Searching Broward County property records

Start with the Official Records search run by the Broward County Records, Taxes and Treasury Division. It is an Acclaim-based system, and you accept a short disclaimer before you can search.

There are nine ways in: party name (grantor or grantee), book and page, document type, instrument number, case number, consideration range, date recorded, parcel ID, and a simple search with plain-language prompts such as a copy of your deed. If all you need is a quick answer on whether a lien has been recorded against you, the simple search is the fastest place to begin.

How far back the online records go

Everything recorded on or after July 7, 1977 is fully searchable online, and plats and maps can be looked up at any date.

Anything older is harder to reach:

  • March 9, 1972 through July 7, 1977: searchable only by instrument number, book type and book and page range, or record date.
  • Before March 9, 1972: not on the site.

If your Broward house has stayed in one family since the 1960s, plan on an in-person request or a title company search to cover the oldest links in the chain of title.

The recording office and bulk data

Recording sits inside the county's Records, Taxes and Treasury Division, and the phone number for questions is 954-831-4000. Call before you mail a deed so you know the exact amount due.

The division also hands out bulk data: 10 continuous days of Official Records files, with images and index data, at no charge. It lists electronic recording vendors too, for firms that file many documents. One homeowner will rarely use either, though a title company working your closing may well e-record.

What it costs to record a deed

Clerk charges are set by Florida statute, and the lines in this table come from s. 28.24(13). Other charges can be added, so ask the Broward recording office for the final total before you send anything.

Statutory recording lines, Florida s. 28.24(13)

Each added page$4.00

Technology charge per page$4

Documentary stamp tax on a Broward deed

Broward uses the standard state rate, $0.70 for every $100 of the price and debt transferred. Neighboring Miami-Dade has its own rates, which do not apply here.

Any mortgage on the property is counted as consideration, even when the buyer takes the house without assuming it. Both sides remain liable no matter what the sales contract says about who pays, and leaving a deed unrecorded doesn't make it untaxable.

  • Taxed: warranty, special warranty, quit claim and trustee's deeds, along with deeds in lieu of foreclosure and certificates of title.
  • Exempt: a spousal homestead deed where a mortgage is the only consideration, and a divorce deed for the marital home.
  • Lady bird deeds: in a 2020 advisement the Department of Revenue found one outside the tax on the facts presented, since no present beneficial interest passed.

Guarding against deed fraud

The Broward County Property Appraiser offers a free Owner Alert service. You subscribe, and it notifies you when the appraiser's office receives a document that changes ownership of your property.

The alert covers ownership changes and nothing else. It suits an owner who is moving out of the area, or heirs holding a vacant inherited house. For questions about recording a deed, adding or removing an owner, or getting copies of recorded documents, use the appraiser's FAQ page: type deed in the questions box and pick the topic closest to your situation.

Property taxes after a sale

When ownership changes, assessed value is reset to full market value and the new owner's bill can jump. The Save Our Homes cap a long-time seller enjoyed does not move with the house.

The appraiser doesn't send bills or collect tax. Billing and collection belong to the Broward County Tax Collector, listed by the appraiser at (954) 357-4829 and revenue@browardtax.org. A seller who is buying another Florida home may be able to carry part of the homestead benefit over through portability, as long as the new homestead is established within three years of the first of January in the year the old one was abandoned.

Liens and foreclosures in the records

Search by party name and again by parcel ID. Liens can attach to the person as well as to the land, and one search alone can miss them. A court sale ends with a certificate of title, and ten quiet days confirm it (s. 45.031).

Someone seeking a tax deed has to wait two years from April 1 of the certificate year before applying. The tax collector lists everyone who has to be notified, including mortgagees and contract-for-deed vendees (s. 197.502).

Filing the deed after closing

A title company can send the deed electronically through one of the county's listed e-recording vendors. If you are filing by hand, phone 954-831-4000 before you go.

Before filing, verify three details: the grantor's name matches the last recorded deed, the legal description is copied exactly, and the two required witnesses have signed (s. 689.01). Choosing not to file saves nothing, since the stamp tax applies to the deed either way.

  • Pull the parcel ID from the appraiser's site.
  • Get the recording charges and stamp tax in the amounts the office quotes.
  • Write down the instrument number once the deed is recorded. The Broward search supports instrument number lookups, and you will want it for any later copy.

After recording, ask for a conformed or certified copy and store it with your closing papers. Buyers, lenders and later title searches all rely on that recorded instrument.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Records and an inherited house

Try the decedent's name every way it might appear: nicknames, married names, whatever was used on a deed or loan. Watch for mortgages that were paid off but never released. Plats and maps are searchable at every date range, so a lot-line question can be checked there. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable for stamp tax, and Florida has had no estate tax for deaths after 2004.

Summary administration may fit an estate of $150,000 or less in non-exempt assets, or an owner dead more than two years (s. 735.201). Creditor claims face a cutoff set by s. 733.702. The title insurer will probably want these steps finished before it insures a buyer.

Foreclosure and your title search

Under s. 702.10 a lender can ask the court for an order to show cause. The hearing then waits for the later of 20 days after the order is served or 45 days after the complaint is served. When a sale has already taken place, the records will show a certificate of title.

Owner-occupied homes are carved out of the quick payment-or-vacate order, and a homestead exemption on the latest roll is a rebuttable presumption of owner occupancy.

If you are behind on a mortgage and thinking of selling, pull your own record first. Knowing what has been filed against the parcel lets you and a buyer, including a cash buyer who skips lender underwriting, plan around the real picture.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Broward County recording office?

It is the Records, Taxes and Treasury Division of Broward County, reachable at 954-831-4000. The Official Records search has its own site.

Are all Broward deeds searchable online?

No. Documents from July 7, 1977 forward are fully searchable. Records from March 9, 1972 to July 7, 1977 need an instrument number, book and page, or record date, and earlier ones aren't on the site.

What is the Florida deed stamp rate in Broward?

It is $0.70 for every $100 of the price and debt transferred under s. 201.02. Every party is liable, and the tax is collected at filing.

Is there a free alert for deed filings on my Broward home?

Yes. The Broward County Property Appraiser offers Owner Alert, which notifies you when a document changing ownership of your property reaches that office.

Does my assessment cap pass to the buyer?

No. A change of ownership resets assessed value to just value the next first of January. Exceptions cover things like transfers between spouses.

Where Hillsborough County property records are kept

Deeds, mortgages and liens for the county go into the Official Records, maintained by the Clerk of Court and Comptroller. Roughly 2,000 new documents are added each day. Search the index from 1965 to today for free through the clerk's Official Records public search.

Older material lives in the Official Records Library, which holds items going back to 1836. The clerk also hosts an archive of deed indexes from 1948 to 1957 and Official Records indexes from 1958 to 1966, along with subdivision plats, tax rolls from 1883 to the present and judgments. Library staff will run a search and prepare a Clerk's Certificate for a fee. A Declaration of Domicile is recorded for $10 at Room 140, 401 Pierce Street in Tampa.

How to search Official Records for a house

Look up the owner by name, then read down the list of instruments for deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, liens and easements. A thorough search before a sale tells you who holds title and which loans or claims are still attached.

  • Begin with the current owner and work back through each earlier deed.
  • Confirm there is a recorded satisfaction for every mortgage you believe was paid.
  • Watch for lien filings, easements and notices of commencement left by recent work.
  • Order a certified copy if a lender or title company wants one.

Copies run $1.00 per page, and certification adds $2.00 per document. For round-the-clock service, the eCertify system sends a self-validating electronic certified copy as a PDF by email. In person at the Records Library, the charge is $2 for each year searched, $1 per page and $2 for certifying.

Hillsborough County recording fees

The first page of a recording is $10.00 and each added page is $8.50. Four names are included, and every name past four adds $1.00. Section 28.24 of the state statutes builds these totals from a $5.00 base for page one and $4.00 for later pages, plus a modernization charge and a $4 per page technology charge.

An online Deed Calculator on the clerk's site gives a complete figure that includes the state tax collected at recording. Every party to the deed owes that tax, whichever side agrees to pay it.

What are the witness rules for recording a deed?

Since January 1, 2024, deeds and similar instruments need two witnesses, each with a printed name and a post office address. The address must be a physical one or a post office box. An email address will not do.

Florida law requires a conveyance of land to be in writing and signed in front of two witnesses. A document missing the witness information can be rejected under section 695.26, and the clerk sends it back with a notice of rejection. The rule reaches deeds, easements, affidavits of interest in land, and agreements, notices or memorandums for deed.

  • Print or type each witness's name and address clearly beside the signature.
  • Have the signed, notarized original ready, since the clerk accepts originals only over the counter or by mail.
  • Attach a transmittal form or cover letter and a prepaid return envelope.

How fast can a document be recorded?

Only a visit in person guarantees same-day recording. Documents mailed in or sent through an e-recording vendor are handled in the order received, and the clerk makes no promise of same-day or next-day service for them.

The recording department takes mail at P.O. Box 3249 in Tampa and walk-in customers at the Downtown Tampa, Brandon and Plant City locations. It also publishes a list of e-recording vendors as a courtesy, without endorsing any of them. The office number is (813) 276-8100. If a closing has a firm deadline, have the title company record in person or through its own e-recording account. A separate consumer portal exists for notices of commencement only, and a mailed notice of commencement can take up to 7 business days to be validated and indexed.

Records that matter at a sale

The deed chain, open mortgages, recorded liens, and any easement or notice of commencement decide how smoothly a closing runs. The title company reads the same index before it issues a policy, so a lien you find first is one you can pay off first.

  • Deed correction: the clerk suggests a real property attorney for adding, removing or fixing a name. Recording costs $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each added page.
  • Quitclaim: Florida statute 689.025 contains a quit claim form, but deputies cannot give legal advice and a quitclaim may not suit every transaction.
  • Lost deed: buy a certified copy through eCertify.
  • Privacy: a social security number can be removed from an image on the clerk's website on written request, at no charge.

Death certificates, military discharges and family or probate court papers are kept off the public website under section 28.2221. A web subscription at $100 a year opens those images to eligible users.

Before listing, print the chain of title and mark any mortgage that lacks a recorded satisfaction. Call the lender for a release if one is missing, since a buyer's title company will find the gap anyway. Gather the survey, any permit paperwork and old closing papers into one folder for the closing agent. A cash buyer has no lender to satisfy, but the title search still happens, so clearing liens early keeps the closing date.

How records connect to property tax

The recorded deed starts a chain that ends on the tax bill. After a deed is recorded, the property appraiser updates the owner on the roll, and the Hillsborough County Tax Collector's bills follow that ownership.

A sale or other transfer of title resets the assessment to just value on the following January 1. Transfers between spouses and some transfers at death are excepted. Deeds in lieu of foreclosure, quit claim deeds and contracts for deed are also taxable documents. A deed is taxable whether or not it is recorded, and tax on an unrecorded taxable document goes to the state rather than the clerk. A deed signed by a personal representative under a probated will is listed as not taxable. For the bill itself, see our Hillsborough County property tax guide.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I search Hillsborough County property records?

Use the Official Records public search from the Hillsborough County Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller. The index from 1965 forward is free online, and older records go through the Official Records Library.

What does it cost to record a Hillsborough County deed?

The clerk charges $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each added page, plus $1.00 for every name after the fourth. Deed documentary stamp tax is separate, at 70 cents for each $100 paid.

Can I email a deed to the Hillsborough clerk?

No. The original signed and notarized deed has to be delivered in person or by mail. E-recording through a vendor is another route, though same-day recording is not promised for it.

What witness details must a Hillsborough County deed show?

Two witnesses, each with a printed name and a physical or post office box address. Missing details can get the document rejected, and an email address does not count as an address.

Where can I order a certified copy of a Hillsborough deed?

The clerk's eCertify service sells certified copies online at any hour and emails a PDF. The office also takes requests in person. Certification adds $2.00 per document to the $1.00 per page copy charge.

The Orange County Comptroller's Official Records Department records, indexes and archives the county's recorded documents: deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, claims of lien, final judgments and orders, notices of commencement and declarations of domicile.

For a seller, this is where the paper trail on a house lives. Before closing, the buyer's title agent will comb it for any mortgage, lien or judgment tied to your name or parcel. Reading the same index yourself before you list shows what that agent will find.

  • Deeds and mortgages show who owns the parcel and who lent against it.
  • Satisfactions show a loan was paid off and released.
  • Claims of lien can come from contractors or associations and must be cleared before a clean sale.
  • Final judgments may be recorded against an owner.
  • Notices of commencement signal recent construction work.

Which office keeps which record?

Recorded land documents sit with the Orange County Comptroller. A different office runs the circuit and county court case files. In Florida the clerk of the circuit court records documents and collects documentary stamp tax at recording, and in Orange County the Comptroller's Official Records Department does that work.

The Property Appraiser is a third office. It keeps the ownership, value and exemption record for each parcel and offers property search, a tax estimator, forms and tax roll information. The Tax Collector bills and collects the tax. A question about a recorded deed or lien starts with the Comptroller. A question about assessed value or a homestead exemption starts with the Property Appraiser.

Go to the Official Records page at occompt.com and run the index search by owner name or by the parcel's legal description. Search every name that has ever been on the deed, including a spouse or a trust, because a lien recorded against a former owner can still sit on the chain of title.

Compare what you find with the Property Appraiser's parcel record so the legal description, the owner of record and homestead status line up. A mismatch in a mailing address, a surname or a legal description is easier to fix before a buyer is waiting. If a recorded item looks wrong or unfamiliar, ask the Official Records Department how to get a certified copy, and ask a title company or a Florida attorney what it means for your sale.

Treat a search screen as a pointer to the recorded instrument. Get a certified copy from the Comptroller when a lender, court or title agent needs a formal one.

A filing adds up from page charges plus documentary stamp tax, and the stamp tax usually outweighs the page charges. The state deed rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and only Miami-Dade runs a different schedule, so Orange County uses the standard rate.

Every party to the document is liable whoever agrees to pay, and the tax is gathered at the recording counter. Consideration counts money, the discharge of an obligation and any mortgage or encumbrance, whether or not the buyer assumes it.

You scan the document and upload it through the vendor's application, and the original stays with you. Funds for transfer taxes, recording fees and a small vendor fee move by ACH. Tax certificates and tax deeds

If taxes stay unpaid, the Tax Collector sells a tax certificate. A certificate left unredeemed for two years can lead to a tax deed application. Orange County processes tax deed sales through the Comptroller's Office, and the Official Records Department runs the auctions.

State law has the clerk hold the public auction. The high bidder posts a nonrefundable deposit of 5 percent of the bid or $200, whichever is greater, and the rest of the money plus recording charges is due within 24 hours, excluding weekends and holidays. An owner behind on taxes should settle with the Tax Collector well before this stage. A tax deed payoff is a separate figure from an ordinary current-year bill, so ask for the redemption total.

Orange County had 1,528,002 residents on July 1, 2025, a 6.9 percent gain over the 2020 base, with 614,386 housing units and 13,140 building permits issued during 2025. Just over 56 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and the median home value is $390,100, across 902.02 square miles of land. That mix of owners, renters and new construction explains why a search here often turns up notices of commencement, association liens and several mortgages on one chain of title.

Using the records to sell faster

Pull your own records first, then clear what you can. A recorded mortgage with no matching satisfaction, an old contractor claim or an unreleased judgment can each stall a closing for weeks.

  • Search the index under every owner name and any prior spelling.
  • Confirm each paid-off loan shows a recorded satisfaction.
  • Ask the Property Appraiser to correct a wrong mailing address or exemption record.
  • Check with the Tax Collector that no current or past taxes are open.
  • Hand your title agent the list so surprises surface early.

If the title is messy and you want to sell as is, a cash buyer can often work around some of these items, though liens are still paid from the proceeds. Compare any offer with the payoff figures in your own records.

What the title agent does after you sign

After the signing, the title agent confirms the payoff figures, disburses funds and sends the deed for recording. Ask for a copy of the recorded deed once it is indexed, and keep it with your settlement statement. If a lien or mortgage payoff is part of your closing, ask for proof that the release was recorded, then search the index a few days later to confirm it appears. This takes a few minutes and avoids a surprise years down the road when you refinance or sell another property.

Who covers the deed stamps in Orange County?

Every party to the document is liable, whichever side agrees to pay. Your sales contract decides who actually pays. The rate is 70 cents for each $100 of consideration.

Is Orange County's Official Records the same as court records?

No. The Official Records Department keeps recorded instruments such as deeds, liens and recorded judgments. Court case files are kept by the clerk of the courts. Ask the right office for the right record.

Can I record a deed online in Orange County?

Yes, through the approved eRecording vendors the Comptroller lists. You upload a scan, pay taxes and fees by ACH, and documents are typically recorded the same day when sent during regular business hours. Call 407-836-5111 with eRecording questions.

Do open tax balances hold up a sale in Orange County?

Where Duval County keeps its records

That department answers at (904) 255-2025, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., except holidays. The recording desk is a separate department at (904) 255-2000, with the same hours.

How far back the online search goes

The online portal covers documents recorded since 1988, plus marriage licenses recorded since February 1981. Anything older needs a request to the Official Records and Research staff.

For a pre-1988 document, give as much detail as you have, such as party names and dates, and bring it to Room 1253 or mail it with a self-addressed stamped envelope. Older deeds for long-held Jacksonville parcels can fall into that earlier set, so start the request well before you need the document at closing.

What copies and searches cost

Viewing and printing uncertified copies from the portal is free, and paper copies from the office cost $1 per page. Certified copies carry the $2.00 certification fee set by Florida law.

  • Payment by mail: money order, business check or cashier's check payable to the Duval Clerk of the Circuit Court. Personal checks are not accepted.
  • E-recording: submissions go through a third-party vendor, and the clerk doesn't endorse any of them.

The clerk processes documents in the order received but can't promise same-day or next-day recording for mail or e-recorded items. If timing matters for a closing, record in person at the Recording Department. Keep the recorded copy and instrument details with your closing papers. Before you go, make sure every signer's name is typed under the signature and that the notary block is complete, since an incomplete page can slow the desk down.

Recording taxes on a sale

Deeds in Duval carry documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration, the rate used everywhere except Miami-Dade. The clerk collects it when the deed is recorded.

Every party to the document is liable under the revenue department's rule, whichever one agrees to pay. Consideration includes money paid, a discharged obligation and any mortgage on the property, assumed or not. A foreclosure certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid. Personal representative's deeds under a probated will are not taxable, but the state says there is no exemption for estate planning transfers in general.

Mortgage tax is 35 cents per $100 secured. The statute also sets recording charges of $5.00 for a first page and $4.00 for each added page, with extra per-page modernization and technology charges on top. Ask the recording desk for the all-in figure for your document.

The office charges $2.00 for each year's search, which is small next to a closing delay. Ask the Property Appraiser about homestead status, since the clerk refers those questions out.

Spotting a fake deed

The clerk offers a free Property Fraud Alert that notifies registered users when a document is recorded in their personal or business name. Scammers record fake deeds to appear as owners and then rent or sell homes that are not theirs.

Vacant houses and inherited homes are the usual targets in a large county like Duval. If you own a rental or an empty property in Jacksonville, sign up before you list it, and recheck the Official Records search whenever a buyer's title company reports something unexpected.

Notice of Domicile

It is a sworn statement that you intend to keep a Florida home as a permanent residence, filed under section 222.17 of the Florida Statutes. The Duval clerk can issue one only for Duval County.

No. By mail the clerk takes a money order, business check or cashier's check payable to the Duval Clerk of the Circuit Court.

Documents go through third-party vendors the clerk lists, split into direct submitters for high volume and indirect submitters for lower volume. The clerk can't recommend or endorse any of them.

One clerk for 24 cities

Fees when a Pinellas deed is recorded

Recording fees follow state law, and the deed itself may owe stamp tax. The clerk posts a PDF at mypinellasclerk.gov/Home/Fee-Schedule that describes its charges as coming from statute, county ordinance and administrative order.

Under section 28.24(13) of the Florida Statutes, page one of an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches is $5.00 and each later page is $4.00. Extras include $1.00 per name past four, a modernization trust fund charge of $1.00 plus $0.50 per added page, and a technology charge of $4 per page.

A 2020 Department of Revenue advisement examined a lady bird deed in which the life tenants kept full powers, and found that no present beneficial interest passed and no stamp tax was due on those facts. That guidance covers one fact pattern, so a title attorney should review yours.

Reading what you find

A recorded document has a few parts worth reading slowly. The top shows who recorded it and when. The body names the parties and describes the property. Title companies work from the same public records you can search, but they read them with a checklist. Taxes due when a deed or mortgage is recorded

Documentary stamps are collected when the deed is recorded: 70 cents for each $100, or part of $100, on warranty deeds, quit claim deeds and comparable transfers. The clerk forwards the money to the Department of Revenue.

Mortgages work differently. Intangible tax on a note secured by a mortgage is paid at recording at 2 mills, or $.002 per dollar financed. The Department of Revenue adds that documentary stamps on a mortgage and note run 35 cents per $100 secured, with a $2,450 cap on a note and no cap on a mortgage.

Everyone named on a document is liable for its tax, whichever party agrees to pay. Many Lee County purchase contracts put the deed stamps on the seller, but the contract is what settles it. State guidance treats an estate representative's deed under a probated will as not taxable and exempts a divorce deed for the marital home.

Recording a death certificate or other documents

It can be done, with conditions. An uncertified copy of a death certificate cannot be recorded unless a court or the Attorney General orders otherwise. A Florida certificate offered for recording has to be a certified copy approved by the Department of Health that omits confidential cause-of-death details. One that includes the cause of death will be refused.

Out-of-state death certificates must be certified copies from that state's agencies or courts. Heirs selling a parent's Lee County house usually need this paper, so request a recordable version at the start. Order several copies, since the county keeps the one it records and a title company may want its own. Ask the Florida Department of Health, not the clerk, how to get the version without the cause of death.

Some rules cover every recording. Names must read the same in the body of the document and under each signature. Any instrument moving an interest in real property, mortgages aside, must show the grantee's mailing address. Wills, plats, court orders and instruments signed outside Florida are treated as exceptions to some formatting rules. Documents mailed without a stamped return envelope are held, and anything still held after 90 days is destroyed.

Foreclosure and eviction filings

Filing a foreclosure or other real property case costs $470.00 when the claim is below $50,000, $975.00 from $50,000 to $250,000 and $1,975.00 above $250,000. The clerk charges $70.00 to hold the judicial sale and asks for a $600.00 deposit toward the notice of sale.

A recorded lis pendens tells buyers that a lawsuit touches the parcel. By statute the sale comes 20 to 35 days after judgment, and an electronic auction is allowed. An owner behind on a mortgage can try for a pre-sale deal that pays off the loan from the sale proceeds.

Eviction filings in county court cost $185.00, and the sheriff's fee for a writ of possession is $90.00, subject to change by the sheriff. A landlord selling a rented Lee County house should expect the buyer to request lease copies, so pull them before listing. Buyers also ask whether any tenant has been served a notice, and the answer should match the court docket.

Steps before you sign a Lee County deed

A short routine keeps a sale from stalling at the recording counter.

  1. Get the legal description from your current deed and copy it exactly.
  2. Confirm every seller and buyer name, spelled as it will appear in the signature blocks.
  3. Line up two witnesses and a notary for the signing.
  4. Decide who pays the stamp tax and write that into the contract.
  5. Ask the title company whether it will record electronically or whether you must deliver the original.
  6. Keep a copy of the recorded deed once it posts.

A cash sale skips lender underwriting, so the deed and the recording paperwork often become the slowest remaining pieces. Having them right the first time saves that time.

Frequently asked questions

Who records deeds in Lee County, Florida?

The Lee County Clerk of Court, through Official Records Services. Filing is available in Fort Myers, in Cape Coral, by mail, by drop box or electronically.

How many witnesses does a Lee County deed need?

Two. The checklist also asks for a full notary acknowledgment, a prepared-by line, and mailing addresses for sellers and buyers.

What is the Lee County recording fee?

Standard recording runs $10.00 for page one and $8.50 for each page after, with $1.00 for each name over four. Deed documentary stamps are billed separately at $0.70 per $100.00.

Can I record an uncertified death certificate in Lee County?

No, unless a court or the Attorney General orders it. The certificate must be certified, and a Florida one must leave out confidential cause-of-death information.

Will the Lee County clerk mail back my recorded document?

Only if you enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope. Otherwise the clerk holds it, and anything held longer than 90 days is destroyed.

Where Pasco County records are kept

The Pasco County Clerk and Comptroller holds the Official Records. Deeds, mortgages, liens and recorded civil judgments are all filed in that single series, and the clerk's website is where you search it. Because judgments go in the same place, a judgment against a seller can surface in a title search.

Two judicial centers handle in-person business. The Robert D. Sumner Judicial Center is at 38053 Live Oak Avenue, Suite 207, Dade City, phone (352) 521-4542. The West Pasco Judicial Center is at 7530 Little Road, Suite 105, New Port Richey, phone (727) 847-8031. Mail goes to P.O. Box 338, New Port Richey, FL 34656-0338. Weekday hours run from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, closed on holidays.

Ownership and assessment data live elsewhere. The Pasco County Property Appraiser runs a parcel search, and its Sale Instrument Type page explains the deed codes you will see in a sales history.

Recording charges at the Pasco clerk

The clerk's FAQ prices page one at $10.00 and each page after that at $8.50. Those totals match the statute, which sets base charges of $5.00 and $4.00 and adds a trust fund charge and a $4 per page technology charge.

Documentary stamp tax on a deed is a separate bill. The statute sets it at seventy cents per $100 of consideration, except in Miami-Dade, and the revenue department says every party to the document is liable no matter who agrees to pay. The clerk takes it at the counter as the deed is recorded.

Page size and the number of parties can move the total. Florida's statute adds $1.00 for every name beyond four, and a different rate applies to instruments larger than 14 by 8.5 inches. If your document is unusual, ask the clerk for a quote before you submit it.

Deeds and transfers that owe stamp tax

Most do, recorded or not. The revenue department's list treats warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's, life estate and in-lieu-of-foreclosure deeds as taxable, along with agreements for deed and certificates of title.

A few are excused. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is listed as not taxable, and a spousal homestead deed whose only consideration is a mortgage is exempt. The department also says there is no specific exemption for transfers made for estate planning. A lady bird deed gets its own treatment: a 2020 advisement concluded that the deed in question passed no present beneficial interest and owed no stamp tax on those facts. Your facts may differ, so have a closing attorney read yours first.

A deed must be written and signed before two subscribing witnesses, and Florida permits witnessing by audio-video technology. Even a quitclaim between relatives is a change of ownership for assessment, and it can reset a capped homestead value.

  • Taxable: warranty, special warranty, quit claim, life estate, deed in lieu.
  • Not taxable: personal representative's deed under a probated will.
  • Exempt: certain spousal and divorce deeds for the marital home.

Foreclosure sales and probate records

The clerk conducts foreclosure sales online and records the certificate of title that moves ownership. Anyone may bid, but a bidder has to register on the Pasco Realauction site and have a deposit on file with the clerk before the sale.

The deposit must be at least 5 percent of the estimated high bid for each property you hope to win. ACH deposits need four full business days to clear and wires one, while cash or cashier's checks must reach the clerk by 5 p.m. Eastern on the business day before the sale. When no objection is filed, the clerk issues the certificate of title after 10 full days from the certificate of sale, and recording it in the Official Records transfers ownership.

Probate turns assets into cash for beneficiaries and creditors and legally transfers real property. Depositing a will with the clerk costs nothing, and probate cases are filed in circuit court in the county of the decedent's home or property.

Protecting yourself from property fraud

Enroll in the clerk's Property Fraud Alert, which watches for liens, deeds and mortgages recorded in your name. You can sign up on the alert website or by phone at 800-747-4600.

When an alert arrives, run an Official Records search and see whether the document is yours. Notices of commencement and marriage licenses can trigger alerts as well. If a recorded paper is fraudulent, the clerk points you to the Pasco County Sheriff's Office non-emergency number, 727-847-8102.

The Property Appraiser separately takes reports of possible homestead fraud. An owner whose house has sat vacant for months has extra reason to sign up, and a recent Official Records printout is worth keeping in the sale file.

Checking the records before you sell

Pull the Official Records for the parcel and read each recorded item against your deed. The title company will do exactly that at closing, so finding a problem first leaves time to fix it.

  • The vesting deed: do the names and legal description match your records?
  • Mortgages and satisfactions: does each paid loan have a recorded release?
  • Liens and judgments: civil judgments are recorded in the Official Records.
  • Tax status: ask the Pasco Tax Collector, which updates its owner of record from ownership-change notices the Property Appraiser sends.

Record the deed promptly after closing. The fraud alert, the Official Records search and the appraiser's sale instrument page all rely on the document being on file, and a gap between closing and recording keeps the old owner on the notices longer.

Delinquent tax gets a certificate in June and can go to auction after two years, so an old unpaid bill is worth settling before you list. A recorded tax deed application shows that a lien has aged out.

A plain order of operations for the seller

Begin with a search under your own name, then under the property description, and save what you find. Next, ask the tax office for a payoff statement even if you think the bills are paid. Finally, give your title agent the vesting deed, any release documents and the tax information at the same time, so nothing arrives piecemeal.

These steps are identical for a regular listing and for a cash sale. The difference is mostly speed, since a cash purchase skips a lender's underwriting, but the title search and the recording still happen in full.

Frequently asked questions

Who records deeds in Pasco County?

The Pasco County Clerk and Comptroller records them in the Official Records. The Dade City and New Port Richey offices serve walk-in customers on weekdays.

What is the fee for filing a deed with the Pasco clerk?

The clerk charges $10.00 for page one and $8.50 for each page after. A deed also owes the state stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration.

Can I search Pasco County records for liens online?

Yes. The clerk's Official Records search covers recorded liens, deeds and mortgages, and civil judgments are recorded there too. The Property Appraiser's records search covers parcel and sales data.

How do I get a fraud alert on my Pasco County property?

Sign up through the clerk's Property Fraud Alert system, online or at 800-747-4600. The service flags liens, deeds and mortgages recorded under your name.

Does a quitclaim deed in Pasco County owe stamp tax?

Generally yes. The Department of Revenue lists quit claim deeds among taxable documents, and a transfer is a change of ownership that can reset a capped homestead assessment.

The Polk County Clerk of Courts keeps the Official Records. Its Public Records Searches page at polkclerkfl.gov links three searches. Official Records covers deeds, mortgages, marriage licenses, liens and HOA deed restrictions, and you can print uncertified copies at home for free.

The other two searches cover court records and tax deeds. The court search handles civil cases, criminal cases and traffic tickets, with dockets and filed documents. Tax bills come from the Polk County Tax Collector at polktaxes.com. Use the clerk to see what is recorded and the tax collector to see what is owed.

A large county with one recorder

Polk covers 2,011 square miles, 1,798 of them land and 213 water, and holds 17 municipalities. The clerk records for every city and every unincorporated area. A house can sit a long drive from the clerk's offices, so the online Official Records search is the practical way to run a title check without making the trip.

The Florida Department of Revenue says all parties to a deed are liable for the tax, whichever party agrees to pay. Consideration includes a mortgage the buyer takes subject to, assumed or not. Warranty, quit claim and trustee's deeds, a contract for deed and a deed in place of foreclosure are all taxable. A spousal homestead deed whose only consideration is a mortgage is exempt, and so is a divorce deed for the marital home.

Section 689.01 requires a deed to be in writing and signed in front of two witnesses. Ask your closing agent to confirm the witnessing before the document goes to the clerk.

Court fees that matter to a distressed owner

Free home printing covers uncertified copies only. A certified copy adds $2.00 for certification, plus $1.00 for each photographic copy up to 14 by 8.5 inches and $5.00 for a larger one.

A sale is a change of ownership for property tax, so the assessment resets to market value on the next January 1, with exceptions such as a transfer between spouses. Tell your buyer to expect a bill built on the sale value, and ask the Polk property appraiser or tax collector for the current figures on your parcel.

Putting it together before listing

Print the search results, circle anything unresolved and sort it by who can fix it. A lender can record a missing release. A lienholder can give a written payoff. A court clerk can tell you what a judgment says. A title agent can tell you which items a buyer's lender will insist on seeing cleared. Ask early, because each fix has its own turnaround, and several fixes in parallel finish sooner than several in a row. Planning which branch to visit

The offices run from Titusville in the north through Merritt Island and Viera to Melbourne and Palm Bay in the south. Choose the one nearest your title company or your home. Titusville has two sites, South Street and the Parkway Complex, and Palm Bay and Merritt Island close over the midday stretch, so a lunchtime trip to either can fail.

The Property Appraiser is a separate elected office with its own schedule. It posts a holiday and early closure calendar on BCPAO.us, with some branch closings listed by date. Check it before driving over for an exemption question, because a Clerk visit and an appraiser visit follow different calendars.

Is the online Official Records search reliable?

Use it to find documents, and treat what you print as unofficial. The Clerk's notice on the site states that only the records held at its branch offices are the Official Public Records, and that checking accuracy is the searcher's job.

  • Try every spelling variation of a name, since the index matches what was typed at recording.
  • No password or fee is needed to search.
  • Restricted information requires a User Subscription Form for Official Records View, and a renewal fee keeps that subscription active.
  • Copies of recorded documents come only from the Clerk's office.

Sellers should know one more thing. Federal tax lien entries on the site do not match the content of what the IRS filed, so searches cannot be relied on in proceedings about title, sales or foreclosure involving a federal lien. Call (321) 637-2004 for the filed copy.

What the Clerk records

Recordable instruments include deeds, mortgages, liens, contracts, affidavits, subdivision plats, surveys, condominium declarations, bills of sale, judgments, certificates of military discharge and declarations of domicile. Recording happens on payment of statutory fees, and most of the traffic involves real estate.

That breadth explains why a title search turns up more than ownership. A Brevard parcel can show a recorded judgment against a prior owner, or a condominium declaration that governs the building, and either one can affect a sale.

Removing private details from the records site

Two Florida laws from 2021 give people a written path. A request under Chapter 2021-215 asks the Clerk to remove information exempt under sections 119.071 and 119.0714, or an image of a military discharge, a death certificate, or certain family, juvenile or probate matters. It must be notarized, state the statutory basis and confirm you qualify for the exemption.

Names in the Official Records index stay unless the name itself contains a street address, as a trust or company name might. Removal requests go to P.O. Box 2767, Titusville, FL 32781-2767, by fax at (321) 264-5246, by email to fs119exemptionrequest@brevardclerk.us, or in person at a branch.

A separate Chapter 2021-231 notice lets an affected person ask the Clerk to add the identity of a respondent in certain minor-protection injunctions, using the case number and the acclaimuseradmin@brevardclerk.us address.

What the Property Appraiser adds

The Brevard County Property Appraiser site, BCPAO.us, offers in-person help with no appointment needed. It also carries market data pages on median single-family sale prices, median market value by property type and the gap between market and assessed value, along with real property value history.

The site also links to information on Amendment 3, which covers major homestead exemption changes. Read it before you list, since exemption rules decide what a buyer inherits.

Recording fees and deed stamp tax

State statute 28.24 sets the Clerk's recording schedule per page, with small extras for added names and for trust fund and technology charges, so a longer deed costs more than a short one. Ask the Recording Division for a quote based on page count before you mail anything.

Deed stamp tax under statute 201.02 is levied on consideration, which includes any mortgage the buyer takes over. All signers share liability, and the Clerk collects it when the deed is recorded. Estate planning deeds get no special break, while a deed from a personal representative handling a probated estate is on the state's not-taxable list.

What to gather before recording

  • A deed signed before two witnesses, as Florida land conveyance law requires.
  • The parcel number and legal description matching the last recorded deed.
  • Payoff letters for any mortgage or lien your search turned up.
  • The stamp tax figure and a check for the recording total, or an arrangement through the title company.
  • Proof of homestead status, if any, to share with the buyer, since a sale resets the assessed value.

Bring the originals, not copies of signatures, and ask the Recording Division whether it will accept your document before you travel to a branch.

When a recording goes wrong

If a deed is rejected or a release seems to be missing, call the Official Records Department at (321) 637-2004 before you resubmit. Ask what was wrong, whether a corrected page is enough, and whether the fee must be paid again. Write down the name of the person you spoke with and the date. Your title company can often fix a rejected form faster than you can, so loop them in the same day.

A step-by-step title search

  1. Start with the current owner's name and the parcel number from the appraiser's site.
  2. Search the Official Records under each spelling or married and maiden name, then repeat for earlier owners back to a clear chain of deeds.
  3. Note every mortgage, lien, judgment and declaration, and which have a recorded release.
  4. Order certified copies from the Clerk for anything you must rely on, because online images are unofficial.
  5. Raise a federal tax lien with the Official Records Department, since the web index can differ from what the IRS filed.

Finishing this before listing means any unreleased mortgage from an earlier owner surfaces while there is still time to ask the lender for a satisfaction. The Clerk records whatever is presented, so a missing release will not announce itself. Only the search reveals it. Keep a list of each document number you reviewed, because the title company will ask for the same references.

Frequently asked questions

Where does Brevard County record deeds?

With the Clerk of Court and Comptroller, acting as county recorder, at any branch office. The Official Records Department number is (321) 637-2004.

Is the Brevard online records search official?

No. Only the records at the Clerk's branch offices are the Official Public Records, so try all spelling variations of a name and order certified copies of anything you rely on.

Can personal identifiers be taken off Brevard's records website?

Yes, for information the law makes exempt. Send a notarized written request that states the statutory basis, by mail, fax or email to the Clerk.

Does the Clerk's name index drop my name on request?

Not usually. Party names stay in the index unless the name itself contains a street address.

Does a Brevard deed owe documentary stamp tax?

Generally yes. The tax is based on consideration and every party to the document is liable. A deed signed by an estate's personal representative is on the state's list of exceptions.

Looking up Volusia County property records online

Two county sites answer most questions. The clerk's Official Records inquiry returns the index and images of recorded papers dating from April 4, 1988: deeds, mortgages, judgments, marriages, divorces, powers of attorney and probate items. A paper appears only after it has been recorded, indexed, verified and released, so a filing from the last few days may not show yet.

The Property Appraiser's search menu is broader. Choose real property by name, address or alternate key, an advanced search by fields and ranges, personal property, sales, or an interactive map. Real property results export to CSV or a mailing list. Put simply, the clerk shows what was recorded against a parcel, and the appraiser shows what the parcel is, who the roll lists as owner and what has sold nearby.

Clerk charges to record a deed

The first page of an instrument no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches costs $10.00, with $8.50 for every page after that. Names past the fourth cost $1.00 apiece to index. State deed tax comes on top, at 70 cents per $100 of consideration or fraction of it.

What a deed needs before the clerk will accept it

Bring the signed original, since photocopies are refused. The deed checklist sets out the layout and content.

  • Leave a 3 by 3 inch blank box in the upper right corner for the office stamp.
  • Write out the legal description and add the parcel ID number.
  • Print every signer's name under the signature along with a mailing address.
  • Show the grantee's name and mailing address (a mortgage is the exception).
  • Print the preparer's name and address.
  • Have two witnesses sign, each with a printed name and address.

Florida's conveyance statute also calls for two subscribing witnesses and permits witnessing over audio-video technology. Other statutes can affect a given transfer, so an owner with an odd situation should see an attorney. Make the check payable to the Clerk of the Circuit Court.

Ways to record a deed

Four routes are open: walk in at DeLand, use the Daytona Beach drop box, mail it, or e-record through a vendor. The Recording Department is at the courthouse, Room A121, 101 N. Alabama Avenue, DeLand, where papers are recorded and returned while you wait. Questions go to 386-736-5912.

  • By mail: Attention Recording Department, P.O. Box 6043, DeLand, FL 32721, with a stamped return envelope. Acceptable payment is a check, money order, business check or cashier's check.

Tax deed information shows parcels headed to the next courthouse auction, and a Lands Available for Taxes list shows land that drew no bidders. A monthly probate report requires a subscriber login.

On a judicial foreclosure, the fee is $70.00 for conducting the sale and issuing and recording the title. Charges change, so call the clerk's office before you file or pay. A records search costs $2.00 per year searched, and public records assistance is billed by the hour. Two courthouse locations serve the county: DeLand for recording and the Daytona Beach Courthouse Annex for a drop box.

What to verify before a sale closes

Look for open mortgages, liens and judgments in the Official Records and trace the chain of title. Match the legal description and parcel number against the appraiser's file, and fix any gap before you sign. Scan the foreclosure and tax deed pages too.

None of those reports replaces a title search, though they show whether a case has been filed against a parcel or an estate. If you inherited the house, probate filings are among the indexed official records. For past-due taxes or liens, request a payoff from the Volusia County tax collector, and ask your closing agent to confirm it before you accept any offer.

Once the checks are done, closing is simple. You sign the deed before two witnesses and a notary, the title company delivers it to the clerk with the fee and tax, and the recorded copy follows. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the same record checks and payoffs still apply, so start them as soon as you decide to sell.

Ten dollars for page one and $8.50 for each additional page, plus $1.00 per name beyond four. The 70 cent per $100 deed tax is charged in addition.

How old are the records in the Volusia County online index?

They start April 4, 1988 and run to the present. Only released items show, so brand-new filings can lag.

Yes, if you send the original with payment and a stamped return envelope to P.O. Box 6043, DeLand, FL 32721, marked for the Recording Department.

Is e-recording available in Volusia County?

Yes, through Simplifile, Corporate Service Company, eRecording Partners Network and Hopdox. It is faster and cheaper than paper.

How many people must witness a Volusia County deed?

Two, with printed names and addresses under their signatures. The Recording Department at 386-736-5912 can answer questions about unusual documents.

Where Sarasota County keeps its property records

The Clerk of the Circuit Court, whose title also includes Comptroller, holds the Official Records, which is the public file for land paper in the county. Anyone can search the index online, and the title agent on your sale will search it as well.

The online search screen opens to a public access group with no login. Search by last or business name, first name, instrument number, a filing date range, or book and page. The index starts on January 1, 1990, so very old papers need a different route.

A separate tab covers marriage records, plats and condominiums, and property fraud alerts. Certified copies go through their own login, and expect a wait of up to 24 business hours.

Document types a seller should look for

The document type menu runs well past a hundred entries. The ones that matter to a seller are DEED, MORTGAGE, SATISFACTION OF MORTGAGE, CLAIM OF LIEN/LIEN, LIS PENDENS, JUDGMENT, TAX LIEN/MISC and the tax deed entries.

Search your own name before you accept an offer, and watch for these:

  • A mortgage with no satisfaction after it, which means the loan still sits on the house.
  • A claim of lien or notice to owner from a contractor, often the result of unpaid repair work.
  • A lis pendens, a sign of a pending lawsuit that touches the property.
  • A judgment or tax lien under your name that could attach to the house.
  • An easement or restriction a buyer will ask about.

The list also includes probate entries such as letters of administration and personal representative oaths, so an inherited house usually leaves a visible paper trail.

Reading the results screen

A search shows the top 500 records only, so narrow a common surname with a first name or a date range. Every hit carries an instrument number you can use to pull the same paper again later.

Labels follow the clerk's own list, and some are easy to miss when a house has a long history:

  • AGREEMENT FOR DEED, the label for a contract for deed.
  • NOTICE OF HOMESTEAD and DECLARATION OF DOMICILE, which relate to residence claims.
  • WARRANT DELINQUENT TAX and FEDERAL TAX LIEN, which sit against an owner and can shadow a closing.
  • DECLARATION OF CONDO and plat entries, handled on the Plats and Condos tab.
  • MOBILE HOME TITLE RETIREMENT, which matters if a manufactured home became real property.

PROBATE, FAMILY and CONFIDENTIAL are separate type codes, so a case file can show up beside the land records.

Recording fees

The first page of a document costs $10.00 and every page after it costs $8.50, for paper up to 8.5 by 14 inches. Plats are priced separately at $30.00 and $15.00.

A document with more than four names pays $1.00 for each name beyond four. State law stacks a base page fee, a records modernization charge and a technology charge, which is how the clerk arrives at those totals.

Deed stamps and mortgage taxes

The clerk charges 70 cents for every $100 of consideration, the same statewide rate, with no local variation in Sarasota County.

Round the price up to the next $100 first, and the minimum is $0.70. A deed is taxable even if it is never recorded. Each party is liable no matter what the contract assigns, so the state can pursue either side.

The buyer's loan brings its own charges: $0.35 per $100 of the obligation as mortgage stamps, plus $0.20 per $100 as intangible tax, figured on the exact amount with no rounding. These attach to the mortgage, which is recorded after your deed.

Some transfers escape the tax. A probate personal representative's deed is listed as not taxable, and a divorce deed for the marital home is exempt. The clerk wants any exemption visible on the face of the document, so have the closing agent check the wording first.

Extra clerk fees for liens and notices

Some filings trigger extra clerk work. A notice of contest of lien, notice of homestead or notice of interest carries a $7.00 certificate of service, plus certified mail at the current postal rate.

Moving a construction lien to a bond costs $20.00 for the first lien and $10.00 for each additional one, with an $8.50 charge to approve the surety bond. For a broker lien the clerk lists $15.00 first and $7.50 each added.

If you learn of a contractor lien before closing, budget for these fees. Clearing the lien is usually a condition of the buyer's title policy.

Sign up for Property Fraud Alerts, a free service from the clerk. Whenever a deed, mortgage or similar paper is recorded in the county under a name you registered, you get an email.

The search screen has a Property Fraud Alerts tab, and the property appraiser urges owners to register. Enter the owner's name and any business name that holds title, ideally before the house sits empty or changes hands.

If an alert arrives for a filing you never signed, call the clerk and an attorney, and keep the instrument number. If an LLC holds title, register the company name too.

How records connect to the tax bill

Recording the deed is what updates ownership for the tax offices. A deed recorded late can leave the new owner without a bill on time.

Proration is settled on the closing statement. You credit the buyer for the months you owned the house, and the collector takes no partial payment from you. Our Sarasota County property tax guide covers the calendar and discounts.

A sale also ends a long-held Save Our Homes cap, because a change of ownership returns the parcel to just value the next January 1. Transfers between spouses are among the exceptions.

Before you sign a deed

Print your own recording history and keep it beside the contract. A short checklist:

  • Look for open mortgages, liens and judgments tied to your name.
  • Make sure every owner named on the deed can sign.
  • Ask the closing agent whether any stamp exemption applies.
  • Sign in front of two witnesses, as Florida requires when conveying land.
  • Register for fraud alerts before the house sits empty.

For an inherited house, the clerk's file shows whether letters of administration were issued. Summary administration is allowed when the non-exempt estate is $150,000 or less, or the owner died over two years ago.

Steps for a clean sale

A sale goes smoothest when you do the paper work first. Search your name and the property, list every open item, and work with the title company to clear each one before a buyer's deadline arrives. Ask for written payoff letters for every mortgage or lien, and keep the recorded satisfaction numbers once they post.

After closing, the deed is recorded and the stamps are paid from your proceeds or the buyer's funds, as the contract provides. Search the index again a few weeks later and confirm that the deed to the buyer and the satisfaction of your loan both appear. Save a copy of each for your files.

A cash buyer still needs a clean record, and a cash sale skips only the lender's steps.

Every party is liable under state law. The purchase contract assigns the cost, and the closing agent usually collects it.

Yes, for $2.00 a document through the certified copy login. Allow up to 24 business hours.

Does a cash sale change the recording steps?

No. The deed is still recorded and the stamps still apply, and liens still get cleared first.

Where Manatee County deeds and mortgages are recorded

The Manatee County clerk of court also serves as Official Recorder. Deeds, mortgages, liens, leases and payoffs all go to the Recording department in Bradenton, where each item is scanned, stamped with the filing time, added to the Official Records book and indexed by name.

Walk-ins and overnight couriers use 1115 Manatee Avenue West, Bradenton, FL 34205. Regular mail goes to a post office box: Recording, P.O. Box 25400, Bradenton, FL 34206. The phone number is 941-741-4045.

Section 28.222 lists what the clerk files, from deeds and claims of lien to lis pendens notices, judgments and discharge certificates. Three groups matter most to a seller: the deed that proves title, the mortgage and payoff trail, and any lien or judgment that could hold up a closing.

Ways to file with the Manatee County clerk

Choose among three routes: bring the original to the counter, mail it with fees and a self-addressed envelope, or send it through an approved e-recording vendor. A mailed document is recorded on the day it arrives, and the clerk asks for 3 to 5 business days after that for its return.

  • Counter: originals come back to you the same day.
  • Mail: include fees and a stamped return envelope, with the check payable to Clerk of Circuit Court.
  • E-recording: you keep the original and the recorded image comes back electronically. Deeds, mortgages, assignments and satisfactions use this route most.

The clerk does not provide legal forms or drafting help and points owners to an attorney or title company. Section 689.01 calls for a written conveyance signed before two witnesses. Fixing an existing deed, whether by adding a name, dropping one, or moving title into a trust or LLC, takes an entirely new recorded deed.

Recording charges

The clerk's Notice of Commencement example shows a typical instrument costing $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each further page. That adds up under s. 28.24: a base of $5.00 then $4.00, a modernization fee of $1.00 then $0.50, and a $4 technology fee on every page.

Who pays document stamp tax on a Manatee County deed?

Every party to the document is liable, whichever one agrees to pay, and payment runs through the clerk as the deed is recorded. Manatee follows the standard Florida rate of 70 cents on each $100 of consideration.

Consideration includes cash, a discharged debt and any mortgage on the property, assumed or not. State revenue officials treat warranty, quit claim and life estate deeds, among others, as taxable, and they say estate planning transfers have no dedicated exemption. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable.

The clerk refers tax-due questions to the Department of Revenue at 850-488-6800. Under s. 201.02(7), a spousal homestead deed funded only by a mortgage, and a divorce deed for the marital home, are exempt.

Searching Manatee County Official Records

The clerk's website offers a free Official Records search, and you can print your own deed or payoff at no cost. A certified copy runs $1.00 a page plus $2.00 for certification and is ordered through Public Access at 941-741-4040.

Records reach back to the 1850s, and anything recorded before 1978 sits in the Historical Records Library at 941-741-4070. Plat maps as old as 1887 can be viewed in the clerk's plat search. Land surveys are not recorded with the clerk, so ask the surveyor or the mortgage holder.

  • Not shown on public websites under s. 28.2221: military discharges, death certificates, and family, juvenile and probate case documents.
  • Death certificates and family, juvenile and probate documents can be viewed after you register a free account.
  • Military discharges cannot be viewed online, and only the person named may buy copies.

The clerk's free Property Alert sends an email whenever a document is recorded under a name you register. It costs nothing and can flag a surprise lien or a fraudulent deed.

What to confirm in the records before listing

Check three things: a paid-off mortgage shows a recorded satisfaction, no lien or judgment sits under your name, and your deed is complete. After payoff the lender should record a satisfaction or release, and copies become available once it posts.

Owners usually receive the original deed at closing from the seller or title company, and a lost one can be replaced with a recorded copy. A will is filed only after death, through Probate at 941-741-4025, which matters for an inherited house.

A Declaration of Domicile can be recorded with the clerk, but the homestead exemption itself is requested from the Property Appraiser at ManateePAO.gov or 941-748-8208, with Florida's March 1 filing deadline.

  3. Order the title search early so any recorded surprise has time to be cleared.

Other documents the Manatee County clerk records

Beyond deeds, the clerk records Notices of Commencement for building permits, Declarations of Domicile, liens and military discharges. The building department that issued the permit supplies the Notice of Commencement form. Common charges are $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, $1.00 per page for a certified copy with a $2.00 certification, and notary service at $5.00 for the first notarization and $2.50 for each added one.

Bring the completed but unsigned form and valid ID to use the clerk's notary service. Liens are governed by Florida Statute 713, and the clerk suggests an attorney for questions. A Declaration of Domicile can be signed before a notary or in front of a deputy clerk at the Recording department, and it can be mailed or recorded in person.

A DD-214 recorded from 1978 to the present can be copied only by the person it names, in person with photo ID. Anyone else should contact the county veteran services office at 941-749-3030.

Manatee County has grown 17.1 percent since 2020, to an estimated 468,200 people across 743 square miles. Owners occupy 74.3 percent of its 243,784 housing units, and the median owner-occupied home is valued at $391,400. Where activity is this busy, order the title search early.

Which Manatee County office takes deeds for recording?

The clerk's Recording department, at 1115 Manatee Avenue West in Bradenton. You can also mail documents or send them through an approved e-recording vendor. Call 941-741-4045 with questions.

The clerk's printed example is $10.00 for page one and $8.50 for each later page, with stamp tax added where it applies. The fee calculator gives exact totals.

They begin in the 1850s, and anything recorded before 1978 is kept at the Historical Records Library. Military discharges and death certificates are not shown on public websites.

Can the clerk fix a mistake on my recorded deed?

Not by editing it. A correction, name change or trust transfer takes a new recorded deed, and the clerk cannot give legal advice.

Seminole County records at a glance

The county holds 181,187 real property parcels. Of those, 138,250 are residential, 16,439 are condominiums and 6,923 are commercial, and there are 13,489 tangible accounts and 45,960 apartment units. Taxable value totals about $60 billion against roughly $92 billion in market value, a gap that comes from exemptions and assessment limits. Most of the paper that crosses the recording desk in Sanford involves those residential parcels.

The appraiser posts its property data for free in a downloads area, refreshed daily in Excel, Access and several GIS formats. Unusual requests, such as owner names and mailing addresses for every non-homestead home, take 10 business days and may carry a labor fee. Site maintenance runs on Wednesday evenings each week.

Which office holds which record

Three elected offices share the work, and any given paper lives in only one of them.

  • Clerk and Comptroller: keeps the Official Records of recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, plats and maps, and runs tax deed auctions.
  • Property Appraiser: ownership on the tax roll, value, exemptions and parcel data. The office is at 1101 E. 1st Street in downtown Sanford, open weekdays 8 to 5. Customer service is 407-665-7506, and exemption or fraud questions go to 407-665-7512.
  • Tax Collector: bills, payments, installment plans and delinquent accounts.

A request sent to the wrong desk gets redirected, but you lose days. The Official Records hold deeds, mortgages, notices of commencement, liens, condominium declarations, judgments, military discharges, probate papers, satisfactions and plats.

How to file a deed

You can deliver the deed in person, mail it with the fees and a self-addressed prepaid envelope, or send it electronically. The Official Records department is at 1750 E. Lake Mary Blvd., Sanford, FL 32773, phone 407-665-4405. Fees and stamp tax are due when the document is filed.

Electronic submissions are typically recorded in 24 to 72 hours, and the image appears online afterward. Four approved vendors handle eRecording: CSC eRecording, eRecording Partners Network, Hopdox and Simplifile. Send 300 DPI scans as TIFF or PDF, on 8 by 11 pages, with names indexed last name first and no more than 15 documents per receipt.

Some items cannot go electronically and must be mailed or hand delivered: a notice of contest of lien or of bond, a notice of homestead, a transfer of liens to security by bond or cash, a transfer of judgment, and a notice of marketable title that needs a certificate of service.

Clerk recording fees and stamp taxes

The fee sheet covers the stamp and tax lines that go with a deed or mortgage, plus copies and searches. State stamp tax is seventy cents per hundred dollars on a deed and thirty-five cents on a mortgage's secured amount, with a twenty cent intangible tax on mortgages. The per-page base charges follow section 28.24(13), plus trust fund and technology amounts the statute permits.
