Can a flawed deed delay a sale?

Yes. Section 689.01 requires a signed writing with two witnesses, who may appear by audio-video link. A title company will catch a missing witness, but fixing it eats days.

Florida revenue guidance treats quitclaims, deeds that avoid foreclosure and contracts for deed as taxable. Spousal homestead deeds backed only by a mortgage escape the tax, as do divorce transfers of the marital home and an estate representative's deed carrying out a probated will. Estate planning transfers get no blanket exemption, so ask the closing agent before assuming a transfer is free.

Property tax billing and collection

After the appraiser certifies the roll, the collector prints and mails bills in November. Paying that month earns 4 percent off, and the reward steps down to 1 percent in February, then nothing. The deadline is March 31. From April 1 the account is delinquent, payable only in certified funds, and picks up advertising and collection fees. Installment plans are offered, and a missed installment counts as delinquent on April 1.

You can pay online, in person, by check to P.O. Box 630 in Sanford, or by courier at 1101 East First St, Room 1200. When a discount month ends on a weekend or legal holiday, the collector carries it to the next working day for payments delivered to a qualifying location.

The bill combines millage set by taxing authorities with non-ad valorem assessments. Tangible taxes on business furniture, fixtures and equipment, and on rental property, arrive with the real estate bill and earn the same discounts.

Amendment 3 and your tax bill

Voters approved the property tax amendment. The collector stresses that the 2026 bill stays as issued, nobody will receive a revised one, and the effects start with tax year 2027, billed in November 2027.

The valuation date stays January 1. Homestead filing has a regular window from January 1 to March 1 and a pre-file window from March 2 through December 31 for the next year, and the appraiser suggests pre-filing to dodge the lines. The standard homestead exemption reaches $50,000, with the first $25,000 applying to every levy. A buyer is reassessed at just value on the January 1 after purchase.

How a tax deed sale works

The clerk holds the auction and issues the deed to the top bidder. The holder of a tax certificate applies through the tax collector, with no lawsuit and no court order. Such property sells buyer-beware, and the deed carries no promise of clear, marketable title. Questions go to taxdeeds@seminoleclerk.org, and the auction calendar and files are online.

A holder must wait two years past April 1 of the issue year before applying. At the sale the winner leaves a deposit that is not refundable, the greater of 5 percent and $200, and settles the balance within one business day. An owner behind on taxes should clear the account with the collector first.

Checklist before you sell

  • Search the Official Records for your deed and any mortgage, lien or judgment, trying every spelling of your name, since the index is only as accurate as the filings.
  • Make sure every paid-off mortgage has a recorded satisfaction.
  • Ask the appraiser to verify exemptions and parcel data. A parcel split or combination request waits until the current year's taxes are paid.
  • Ask the collector whether this year is paid.
  • List owner names exactly as on the deed for the new instrument.

If an old deed misspells a name, ask the clerk how a corrective instrument is recorded and what it costs. Winter Springs, Oviedo, Lake Mary and every other city in the county use the same recording process. The clerk also offers free property fraud alerts, which the appraiser recommends.

Once the title company has your payoff letters and a clean search, the closing is mostly signatures. You sign the deed before two witnesses, the title company submits it to the clerk, and the stamp tax and recording fee come out of the settlement. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the clerk, the appraiser and the collector still have to be satisfied, so the same records need to be in order whichever way you sell.

The clerk's Official Records department, 1750 E. Lake Mary Blvd. in Sanford. One office serves every city in the county.

What does the Seminole clerk charge to record?

Ten dollars for page one and $8.50 for each page after, with stamp taxes added where the document calls for them.

Does eRecording work for every document type?

No. A handful, including a notice of homestead and a transfer of judgment, have to be mailed or hand delivered.

The clerk. The certificate holder applies through the tax collector first.

The Official Records portal is a separate search tool linked from that page. Search it by party name or document type to see whether a mortgage, lien or earlier deed sits on a Naples, Marco Island or Immokalee property. The clerk's custodian of public records takes requests at 3315 Tamiami Trail East, Suite 102, Naples, FL 34112, phone (239) 252-2646.

What the clerk keeps for a house sale

Any instrument that has to be recorded to protect a buyer lands in the clerk's Official Records, and a title company searches that file before a Collier County closing. Typical contents:

  • Warranty, quit claim and other deeds that moved title to the current owner
  • Mortgages and the satisfactions that release them
  • Plat maps and condominium declarations for the subdivision or building
  • Lis pendens notices filed when a foreclosure case begins

The clerk also posts the foreclosure sale list and the tax deeds list, so a title problem tied to a court case or unpaid tax usually shows up under one of those headings.

Recording charges

Recording in Naples starts at $10.00 for page one of a letter or legal size instrument, then $8.50 for each further page. The statute behind the base charge sets $5.00 and $4.00, and the county's page adds the extra per-page charges the statute allows. The lines below are the ones most sellers meet.

Documentary stamp tax on a deed

State tax on a deed is 70 cents on each $100 of consideration. The Collier clerk collects it at the counter or online as the deed is recorded, and rounds the amount up to the nearest hundred.

The Department of Revenue treats each party to the document as answerable for the tax, whoever agrees to pay. Consideration takes in cash, a discharged debt and any mortgage on the parcel, assumed or not. Deeds are taxable recorded or not, and warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's and life estate deeds are all on the taxable list. A probate personal representative's deed is not taxable.

Mortgages and notes have separate rates. The state sets 35 cents per $100 of the amount secured, matching the clerk's mortgage line, and caps the tax on a note at $2,450 with no cap on mortgages. Your closing agent can run the final figure.

E-recording

A document counts as recorded once the clerk enters it into the Official Records. The office can't promise same-day recording for mail or electronic submissions, so a time-sensitive document belongs at the main office, where it is recorded while you wait.

Pull your own chain of title first, because a clean search saves days at closing. Look up the deed you received, then every instrument recorded against your name since.

A certification costs $2.00 and a search $2.00 per name, instrument or year, so a certified copy of a paid-off mortgage is cheap next to a delayed closing. Liens and unpaid taxes

Unpaid real estate tax becomes a tax certificate, and its holder can later seek a tax deed that the clerk auctions. The clerk's tax deeds list shows which Collier parcels have reached that stage.

Under state law a tax deed application can be filed once two years have run from April 1 of the year the certificate was issued. The county tax collector's site links to an online certificate sale. When you sell, gather the collector's payoff and the clerk's lien search side by side and hand both to the closing agent. Our Collier County property tax guide covers the billing side.

Researching a parcel before you list

The Collier County Property Appraiser runs the parcel search and posts public data files for the whole county or a smaller area at no charge. Pair a parcel lookup with an Official Records search by owner name, and you can match the legal description on your deed against what the appraiser shows.

Before listing, verify three items: the owner name spelled the same on the deed and the tax roll, any mortgage with no recorded satisfaction, and any recorded notice from a court case. A mismatch is easier to fix with the clerk before an offer arrives than during closing week.

If you record the deed yourself

Prepare the signed deed, the parcel number, and payment for the recording charge and stamp tax. Confirm the legal description matches your prior deed, and ask the office for a receipt. After recording, request a copy showing the recording stamp and keep it with your closing file. Buyers and lenders expect that stamped copy, and a cash buyer will want it too, since there is no lender to chase it for them.

The Collier clerk and comptroller. The Recording Department is at 3315 Tamiami Trail East, Suite 102, Naples, and takes calls at (239) 252-2646.

Page one costs $10.00 and later pages $8.50 each, for letter or legal size instruments. Oversize plats cost $30.00 for page one and $15.00 for every page after.

$0.70 per $100.00 of consideration, rounded up to the nearest hundred. Florida makes all parties to the document liable, so the contract decides who pays it.

Yes, in person, with a 3.5% processing fee on each transaction. E-recording with a card carries a 4% fee from the card processor.

Added technology charge$4 per page

Your document's page count and the names on it move the total, so phone the Clerk for the figure that applies to your deed. The stamp tax is paid at that same window.

Check the record before you list

Before you list, pull the vesting deed and anything else recorded in your name. Landmark Web will let you retrace how title reached you by name, book and page, record date or legal description.

  • Compare the legal description on your last deed with the one attached to the tax account at the appraiser.
  • Look for recorded mortgages, liens or court documents that a payoff must clear.
  • Make sure each owner's name is spelled the same way on every instrument.
  • Note whether the parcel is inside Pensacola, Century or the unincorporated county, since that changes which non-ad valorem charges show on the tax bill.

A title agent repeats this search later. If something is off, you want to learn it now, while a fix will not collide with a buyer's deadline.

Documentary stamp tax on a deed

Escambia pays the usual Florida rate: 70 cents for each $100 of the sale price. Miami-Dade is the only county that pays less.

The amount taxed counts cash, a debt that gets wiped out and any mortgage on the land, even one the buyer does not assume. Whoever agreed to cover the tax, every party to the deed stays liable, and the clerk takes payment when the deed goes on record. Mortgages and notes are taxed at 35 cents per $100 secured. A note tops out at $2,450, while a mortgage has no ceiling.

  • Taxable: warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's and life estate deeds.
  • Also taxable: a deed in lieu of foreclosure and an agreement for deed.
  • Not taxable: a personal representative's deed under a probated will.
  • Exempt: a spousal homestead deed where the only consideration is a mortgage, and a divorce deed for the marital home.

What makes a deed recordable

Land can only be conveyed by a written deed with two witnesses watching the signing. Section 689.01 asks for two subscribing witnesses, drops the old seal requirement and permits witnessing over audio-video technology.

Before the paper goes to the Clerk, sit down with your title agent and check four things:

  • The legal description copies the prior recorded deed exactly.
  • Every owner of record signs, each in front of two witnesses.
  • Stamp tax is figured on the correct price.
  • A lawyer has looked at any lady bird deed. In one Department of Revenue advisement such a deed passed no present beneficial interest and owed no stamp tax on those facts, though different facts can change the answer.

Protecting a property from fake deeds

The Clerk's Landmark Web site offers Property Fraud Alert. Enroll a name, and you get an email every time a land records document is filed under it.

The service is free. It only reports recorded instruments and does not stop fraud. Still, an alert on your own name, and on the name of a deceased relative if you inherited the house, gives early warning of a forged deed. If an owner of family property has died and records were never updated, probate or another process may be needed to settle who owns it.

Tax, foreclosure and probate records

Three offices, three sets of files. Tax history is at the Tax Collector, and an unpaid bill goes delinquent April 1, after which a tax certificate can be issued. Foreclosure sales run through the Clerk. State law has the clerk schedule a foreclosure sale from 20 to 35 days after final judgment, and the top bidder leaves a 5 percent deposit.

For a house with probate history, ask the Public Records Center, which holds probate cases back to 1883 for in-person viewing. A shortened estate procedure called summary administration is open when the non-exempt estate is $150,000 or less, or when the decedent died more than two years before.

Marriage records, name changes and closing day

These records help when a signer's name changed or an heir must be proved. Marriage records from 1996 to the present are in the Public Records Center, and older books run back to 1822.

  • Marriage books: 1822 to 1999, viewed in person.
  • Microfiche: 1919 through 1995, plus indexes covering 1821 to 1900 and 1901 to 1918.
  • Records from 1996 forward: available through the Clerk's records service.

If your name differs between the vesting deed and your current ID, collect the marriage or court record that links the two names before you list. Otherwise the buyer's title company may stall the closing.

On closing day, bring photo ID and expect to sign the deed in front of the required witnesses. The title agent sends the signed deed to the Clerk for recording, and the stamp tax goes in with it. Afterward, ask the title agent for the recorded copy and file it with your closing papers. Its recording date and book and page numbers are what any later search will point to.

Frequently asked questions

Where are Escambia County deeds recorded?

At the Clerk and Comptroller's office. The Landmark Web site lets you look up recorded papers by name, book and page, record date and several other fields.

What is the stamp tax on a deed in Escambia County?

The statewide rate of 70 cents per $100 of price. Everyone named on the deed is liable, and the clerk collects when the deed is recorded.

How much is the first page recording fee in Florida?

$5.00 under section 28.24, plus $1.00 for the modernization fund and an added $4 per page technology charge. Each added page is $4.00 plus further charges.

Can I view Escambia County probate files from the 1800s online?

No. Old wills, probate cases from 1883 to 1997 and civil files from 1820 to 1985 can only be viewed at the Public Records Center.

Does Escambia County offer an alert for fraudulent deeds?

Yes. Enroll a name in the Clerk's free Property Fraud Alert and you are emailed whenever a document is filed under it. It reports fraud after the fact and cannot block it.

Where Lake County property records are kept

Deeds, mortgages and liens for Lake County go into the Official Records, which the clerk and comptroller maintains. The clerk's recording section handles deeds, mortgages, satisfactions, liens, powers of attorney, notices of commencement, agreements for deed, plats, judgments, financing statements and death certificates.

The clerk's website has a records search area, a guide to researching Official Records, a tax deed record search and a foreclosure sales calendar. The last two matter if a house has a delinquent history. The Property Appraiser keeps the parcel and ownership side, so a full picture of a house means checking both offices. The county has two clerk locations for in-person recording. Confirm their hours before you plan a closing day trip.

  • Clerk: recorded deeds, mortgages, liens, lis pendens, tax deed files.
  • Property Appraiser: parcel data, owner of record on the tax roll, exemptions.
  • Tax Collector: tax bills and any certificate on the parcel.

Lake County recording fees

Page one of a standard-size instrument costs $10.00, and each page after that is $8.50. Indexing adds $1.00 for every name over four.

The clerk's site also links a fee calculator for deeds and mortgages, worth running before you wire money to a closing agent.

What taxes does the clerk collect when a deed is recorded?

Documentary stamp tax on a deed is collected at recording. The rate is 70 cents per $100 of consideration or fraction thereof, with a minimum of 70 cents on deeds whose consideration is $100 or less.

The tax follows every party to the document, and a deed owes it even if never recorded. An estate representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable, but quit claim deeds, contracts for deed and deeds in lieu are.

Mortgages carry two charges at recording: documentary stamps of 35 cents per $100 on the promise to pay, and a one-time intangible tax of 2 mills, which is .002 per $1. A cash sale with no new loan usually records just the deed, so ask the title company what is going on the record.

How to file a document in Lake County

Everything goes through the clerk's Recording Section, by one of four methods: in person, by mail, by drop box or by eRecording. Documents are recorded in the order received, typically within two business days. Same-day or next-day recording cannot be guaranteed for mail, drop box or electronic submissions.

If timing matters, record in person at one of the two locations. Make checks payable to the clerk and comptroller. Cashier's checks dated more than two months earlier are refused. Visa, MasterCard, Discover and American Express are taken, with a non-refundable processing fee on card payments.

  • Include an "this instrument prepared by" statement, which Florida law requires on the face of conveyances.
  • Use the clerk's Recording Transmittal Form to speed processing.
  • Leave out Social Security numbers unless the law requires them. If one slips in, the clerk will remove it from the online image on a written request, at no charge, which is a useful step for anyone who recorded paperwork years ago.
  • Expect the recorded document back by U.S. first class mail, with an envelope optional.

Can a Lake County owner watch for fraudulent deeds?

Yes. A free clerk service emails you when anything is recorded under a name you list, and each address can watch five names.

Scammers file false deeds to pose as owners and then collect money for rentals or sales. Owners of vacant, inherited or out-of-state houses are the most exposed, because nobody is watching the mailbox. Sign up through the clerk's recording notification service, and check the Official Records search yourself now and then for your surname.

Beyond the alert, keep your own address current with the Property Appraiser so tax notices reach you, and glance at the tax collector's record once a year for charges you do not recognize. Recording order matters too. Documents are recorded as received, so a deed and the mortgage that funds it should arrive together, and the closing agent usually sends them the same day.

Checking the records before you list

Pull the vesting deed and look for open mortgages, judgments, liens and a lis pendens, since each must be paid or released before a buyer gets clear title. A title company runs this search at closing, but running it first avoids surprises.

  • The deed names exactly who owns the house and how they hold title.
  • Any mortgage without a recorded satisfaction.
  • Notices of commencement or liens from contractors.
  • A lis pendens, which signals a lawsuit tied to the parcel.
  • Prior-year tax certificates, checked with the tax collector.

For an inherited house, ask the clerk's probate section what must be on file before the personal representative can sign a deed. A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not on Florida's list of taxable deeds, a useful point to raise with your closing agent.

Print what you find and bring it, with a copy of your deed, to the first call with the title company. If a lien or old mortgage turns up, contact the holder for a release before you accept an offer. A cash buyer will still order a title search, so clearing items early protects your closing date.

How lis pendens and foreclosure show up in the records

A foreclosure suit appears in the Official Records as a lis pendens, priced at $5.00 for page one and $4.00 after. Releasing one costs $10.00 and $8.50.

State law puts the public sale between 20 and 35 days after a final judgment unless the plaintiff consents to longer. The sale notice runs two weeks in a row, and the winning bidder leaves a deposit. The clerk keeps a foreclosure sales calendar on its site, which is the place to confirm any sale date. A homeowner who sees a lis pendens against the house should talk to a Florida attorney, and can still sell before the sale if the payoff is covered.

Frequently asked questions

Does the Lake County clerk record deeds?

Yes. The clerk acts as county recorder, so deeds, mortgages and liens all end up in the Official Records. Recording happens in the clerk's Recording Section.

What will a deed cost to file in Lake County?

Page one is $10.00 and later pages are $8.50 each, with $1.00 added per name past the fourth. Deed stamps are a separate charge.

How long does Lake County recording take?

Documents are recorded in order received, typically within two business days. Same-day recording is not guaranteed for mail, drop box or eRecording, so record in person if the date matters.

Can I record a Lake County document electronically?

Yes. eRecording is one of four ways to record, along with in person, mail and drop box.

Yes. A free email alert goes out when a document is recorded under a name you monitor, and five names fit on one address.

Where Osceola County records are kept

Everything recordable in Osceola County lands at the same counter. The clerk of the circuit and county courts also serves as comptroller and county recorder, and the clerk's website, osceolaclerk.com, carries the recording forms, eRecording, tax deed information and the property fraud alert signup.

Documents go into one running series called the Official Records. Nothing leaves that series unless a court orders it. Parcel values and exemptions are a different matter: those belong to the Property Appraiser at 2505 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway in Kissimmee.

Documents the clerk records

The recording list is broad. It covers deeds, leases, mortgages, liens, judgments and other instruments that affect real or personal property.

  • Deeds, mortgages, notices or claims of lien, plus their releases and satisfactions
  • Lis pendens notices, which announce that a lawsuit touches a property
  • Judgments and their assignments, releases and satisfactions
  • Federal tax liens and the certificates releasing them
  • Certified death certificates and military discharge records

Sellers should pay attention to two entries in particular. A foreclosure case in progress appears as a lis pendens against the parcel. A recorded judgment can attach to any land the debtor owns.

Recording requirements for a deed

A deed that misses the clerk's formal checklist can be returned until it is fixed. The clerk's page points to Florida Statute 695.26 and spells out what the face of the document must show.

  • The grantor's notarized signature, with a printed name and address beneath it
  • Two witnesses with printed names; on documents dated January 1, 2024 or later, their post office addresses too
  • A full legal description
  • The grantee's mailing address, along with the preparer's name and address, written as a person's first and last name and not only a business name
  • A blank 3 by 3 inch area in the top right corner, reserved for the clerk
  • Original ink signatures, because photocopies are refused

The office does not run title searches. It sends people who need one to a title agency or an attorney.

Payment methods, hours and address

Bring a business check, cashier's check, money order or cash. Personal checks are turned away. Credit and debit cards work only at the counter, with a 3.5 percent surcharge.

The Recording Department sits upstairs at the courthouse, 2 Courthouse Square, Kissimmee, FL 34741. The recording line is (407) 742-3517, and the main clerk line is 407-742-3500. Anyone mailing a deed should include a self-addressed, postage-paid return envelope. The clerk also accepts e-recordings.

Searching Official Records and ordering copies

The online Official Records search runs around the clock. For paper, you can buy copies in person, electronically, or through PERCH Search or MyFloridaCounty at $1.00 per page. Each certification adds $2.00, and plat copies cost $5.00 per page.

The cheapest protection available is the clerk's Property Fraud Alert. The office has no way to verify who actually signed a paper placed in front of it, and only a judge can order a bad filing removed. An alert that tells you when something is recorded under your name gives you an early warning while the house is being prepared for sale.

If a bad document appears on your property

Report it quickly. The clerk cannot pull a filing without a court order. Depending on where the home sits, the clerk's FAQ suggests the Kissimmee Police Department, the St. Cloud Police Department or the Osceola County Sheriff's Office, and says a document touching several Florida locations may go to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

Section 817.535 of the Florida Statutes makes recording a fraudulent instrument against property a third degree felony, and a court can order such a document voided and removed. Tell your title agent the moment you find an odd entry. A buyer's lender will not close over a lien or deed nobody can explain.

Tax records and tax deeds

Real estate tax left unpaid in Osceola turns delinquent at the start of April and picks up a 3 percent addition. The collector auctions certificates on those parcels online by June 1, with bids opening at 18 percent and falling from there.

The clerk runs tax deed sales online. A certificate that sits untouched can support a tax deed application from April 1 of the second year after it was bought. If the winning bidder backs out, the deposit is forfeited; it is the greater of 5 percent of the bid or $200, and the balance is due within a day. Tax deed land sells as is, and the clerk warns that no promise of clear title comes with it.

When a sale produces overbid money, the claim is an affidavit sent to the clerk's Tax Deed Department.

Dates on the Osceola tax bill

The Tax Collector's calendar rests on a handful of fixed dates. Payments open in November at a 4 percent discount, step down to 3, 2 and 1 percent through February, and reach the full amount in March.

Requests to join the quarterly installment plan are due by April 30. Installments then fall on June 30, September 30 and December 31. An installment that misses July 31 loses its discount, adds a 5 percent penalty and ends the plan.

  • April 1: delinquent, with 3 percent added to the gross amount
  • Three weeks of newspaper advertising before the certificate sale
  • On or before June 1: online tax certificate sale
  • Redeeming on or after June 1 adds a $6.25 fee

Interest on a sold certificate follows the rate at which it sold, so get the payoff in writing for your own closing day.

Steps before a sale, in order

Search the Official Records under your name and the property description. Read each hit against your deed. Look for any mortgage that was paid but never released, any lien or judgment, and any lis pendens. Fix paperwork gaps first, because a title company will find them anyway and each one can hold up a closing.

Next, check the tax account and ask the collector for a written payoff if anything is open. After closing, confirm the new deed was recorded and keep a stamped copy. If you are comparing a standard listing with a cash sale, these same steps apply to both. A cash sale mainly skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, not the title work.

Frequently asked questions

Which office records deeds in Osceola County?

The Osceola County Clerk of the Circuit Court and County Comptroller, acting as county recorder. The office is at 2 Courthouse Square in Kissimmee and records deeds, mortgages, liens and judgments.

What does it cost to record a one-page deed in Osceola County?

The clerk charges $10.00 for the first page, plus documentary stamp tax of $0.70 per $100 of consideration. Each added page costs $8.50, and names beyond four cost $1.00 each for indexing.

Can I pay with a personal check at the Osceola recording counter?

No. The clerk takes business checks, cashier's checks, money orders and cash, and credit cards in person with a 3.5 percent fee.

What time must I submit a deed in Osceola County?

Before 4:30 p.m. on a business day. The courthouse stays open until 5:00 p.m., but recording stops at 4:30, and later documents are recorded the next business day.

Can the clerk remove a fraudulent deed from the records?

Not on its own. The clerk can remove a recorded item only under a court order. Report suspected fraud to law enforcement, and consider the free Property Fraud Alert.
